subject: Apples to oranges? Trouble calculating AKDEs on a consistent grid

messages.author: e38a81370d305d2c
messages.subject: Apples to oranges? Trouble calculating AKDEs on a consistent grid
parts:
Hi Chris,

I'm very new to home range analyses so I hope this isn't an obvious question. I have a telemetry dataset of 117 lizards. Lizards were tracked 1-2x/day during a ~3 month season each year. A new set of ~30-40 lizards was tracked each year for 3 years. I'm trying to compare the average 95% UD of the population across years. I think I've done everything right– followed the first half of example code at the end of the meta function description. However, although the code should have calculated the AKDEs on a consistent grid, I'm still finding my bandwidths are different (0.5<h<0.7) for each individual when I look at the output dataset. 

1) Is it appropriate to compare across years given these slightly different bandwidths? Are there further analyses you recommend to ensure a fair comparison?
2) I didn't thin my original dataset at all, so there are some individuals with <10 observations (due to slipped collars) and some with 70 observations (collared the entire season). From what I understand, this should be okay for AKDEs. Is that correct or would you recommend excluding lizards below a threshold number of resightings? 

Thank you for any feedback,
Emme

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Apples to oranges? Trouble calculating AKDEs on a consistent grid
parts:
Hi Emme,
  1. Yes, and I realize that there are numerous papers published in wildlife and ecology journals that discuss averaging the bandwidth across individuals, but I've never seen any reference to the statistics literature on KDE to justify this. The individual AKDE bandwidths are optimized to minimize bias and variance, then in AKDEc there is an additional bias reduction, and finally in all comparisons made in ctmm the uncertainties are propagated. Fixing the bandwidth will increase the bias and variance by an unknown amount, and that bias will not necessarily be consistent across individuals, because it depends on both the sampling schedule and the movement characteristics. I think the old arguments for standardizing the sampling schedules make sense with older analyses, but standardizing the bandwidths will under-smooth some individuals while over-smoothing others. I don't see how introducing a mix of positive and negative biases could possibly help anything.
  2. https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.13270
    https://github.com/ctmm-initiative/ctmmlearn/blob/main/ctmm_effective_sample_sizes.R
    The default estimates are pretty good down to effective sample sizes of 4-5, and ctmm.boot() can get you down to 2-3. Since your small-DOF individuals are at random (slipped collars), then it should be safe to throw out the bad estimates to reduce negative bias. [In other cases where all individuals are sampled similarly and the small-DOF individuals correspond to larger movements, throwing out the worst estimates could actually increase the negative bias.]
Best,
Chris
